_schema: piece_id or composer_id -> list of raw facts; LLM turns these into multi-style fun facts

debussy_clair_de_lune: Part of Suite bergamasque; the suite was published in 1905 but some of it was written earlier.
One of the most recognizable piano works globally, used in films and ads.
Debussy was inspired by a poem by Paul Verlaine of the same name.
The piece was not the original third movement—Debussy replaced the earlier 'Promenade sentimentale'.
debussy_arabesque_no1: An 'arabesque' in music suggests flowing, ornamental lines rather than a strict form.
Written when Debussy was in his twenties; the set of two arabesques was published in 1891.
Often used in ballet and figure skating for its light, flowing character.
The piece avoids heavy bass and keeps texture transparent and decorative.
debussy_reverie: Debussy later said he thought little of this piece and was surprised by its popularity.
Published in 1890; the title means 'daydream' in French.
One of his earlier works that already shows his interest in color and atmosphere over strict form.
Frequently used in relaxation and meditation playlists.
chopin_nocturne_op9_no1: A nocturne is a 'night piece'—often lyrical and reflective.
Chopin was in his early twenties when he wrote the Op. 9 set.
One of the most frequently taught and performed piano pieces.
The melody was later adapted into pop songs in the 20th century.
chopin_ballade_no1: Chopin invented the ballade as a standalone instrumental genre.
Inspired by Polish poet Adam Mickiewicz; the music is narrative and dramatic.
Schumann said Chopin had told him the ballades were inspired by Mickiewicz's poems.
The piece builds to a famously difficult and stormy coda.
chopin_prelude_raindrop: The nickname 'Raindrop' comes from the repeated A-flat that runs through the middle section.
Part of the 24 Preludes, Op. 28—one in each key, like Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier.
Written during Chopin's stay at Valldemossa with George Sand during a storm.
The persistent note is said to echo the rain on the monastery roof.
satie_gnossienne_1: Satie invented the word 'Gnossienne'—it has no prior meaning.
He broke rules by adding written instructions in the score like 'open your head' and 'with astonishment'.
Part of a set of six Gnossiennes; the first three were published in 1893.
The piece has no bar lines in the original, giving it a floating, timeless feel.
satie_gymnopedie_1: Gymnopédie refers to an ancient Greek festival where youths danced.
Satie wrote three Gymnopédies; Debussy later orchestrated the first and third.
Extremely simple harmony and rhythm—often one of the first 'classical' pieces people learn.
Used in countless films, ads, and games for its calm, slightly sad mood.
satie_gymnopedie_3: The third Gymnopédie is slightly more active than the first but still very calm.
Like the others, it uses a slow 3/4 time and simple, repeating chords.
Satie was known for his humor; he once described himself as 'a musician in the medieval sense'.
rachmaninoff_piano_concerto_2: Written after a period of depression; the composer credited his doctor with helping him recover.
The famous opening chords are said to represent the tolling of bells.
One of the most popular piano concertos ever written.
The second movement was used in the film 'Brief Encounter' and many others.
rachmaninoff_rhapsody: Variation 18 is the 'big tune'—often played on its own in films and concerts.
Based on a theme by Paganini; Rachmaninoff turns it into a romantic love song.
The composer wrote it at his summer home in Switzerland.
It was featured in the movie 'Somewhere in Time'.
rachmaninoff_prelude_op23_no5: Part of a set of ten preludes; he wrote preludes in all 24 keys across two opus numbers.
This one is nicknamed 'Alla marcia' for its march-like character.
Rachmaninoff had very large hands and could span huge chords—this piece uses that.
Often used as an encore for its short, brilliant effect.
schubert_ave_maria: The text is from Walter Scott's 'The Lady of the Lake,' not the traditional Latin prayer.
Schubert never called it 'Ave Maria'—that title was added later.
One of the most recorded classical pieces, in classical and pop arrangements.
Originally for voice and piano; now often heard with orchestra or organ.
schubert_impromptu_op90_no3: An 'impromptu' suggests something spontaneous, though the piece is fully composed.
The main melody is in the middle voice, with flowing accompaniment above and below.
One of four impromptus in D. 899; this set was published after his death.
Often described as a 'waterfall' or 'cascade' of notes.
schubert_serenade: From the song cycle 'Schwanengesang' (Swan Song), assembled after his death.
The singer addresses a lover under the window—a classic serenade scenario.
The piano imitates a guitar or lute in the accompaniment.
Extremely popular in transcriptions for cello, violin, and piano solo.
shostakovich_waltz_no2: From a 'Suite for Variety Orchestra'—often mistaken for the Jazz Suite.
The waltz has a nostalgic, sometimes ironic tone typical of Shostakovich.
Widely used in film and advertising for its catchy, cinematic feel.
The 'variety' orchestra is smaller than a full symphony orchestra.
shostakovich_symphony_5: The composer said the finale was 'the forced rejoicing of someone threatened with torture'.
Written in 1937 after his opera was condemned; it was a public rehabilitation.
The symphony was a huge success and was seen as a 'Soviet artist's reply to just criticism'.
The opening is one of the most dramatic in the repertoire.
shostakovich_piano_concerto_2: Written for his son Maxim's graduation from the Moscow Conservatory.
The second movement is one of his most lyrical, romantic pieces.
Uses a smaller orchestra (no violins in the slow movement).
Often considered more 'accessible' than his darker symphonic works.

debussy: He hated the term 'impressionism' and did not want to be grouped with painters like Monet.
He was a notorious procrastinator and often missed deadlines.
He loved the sea and wrote 'La mer' after spending time by the ocean.
His daughter was named Claude-Emma; he called her 'Chouchou' and wrote a piano suite for her.
chopin: He almost always composed at the piano and left very few non-piano works.
He preferred intimate salons to large concert halls and gave few public concerts.
He was close friends with Delacroix and had a famous portrait painted by him.
His heart was buried in Warsaw; his body is in Père Lachaise in Paris.
satie: He once owned a collection of identical gray velvet suits.
When his room was opened after his death, two pianos were found, one with unopened mail inside.
He was a café pianist for years before gaining recognition.
He founded his own church and was its only member—'Metropolitan Art Church of Jesus the Conductor'.
rachmaninoff: He was also a famous conductor and made many recordings as pianist and conductor.
He had enormous hands and could span a 13th on the piano.
He left Russia after the Revolution and never returned.
He was a fan of jazz and met Gershwin; he admired 'Rhapsody in Blue'.
schubert: He wrote over 600 songs and many were only published after his death.
He died at 31; his cause of death is still debated.
He was part of a circle of friends who held 'Schubertiads'—private concerts of his music.
He never held an official position and lived mostly from teaching and publishing.
shostakovich: He lived under Stalin and had to balance artistic truth with political survival.
His music often contains hidden messages and irony that Soviet censors missed.
He was a passionate football (soccer) fan and followed Zenit Leningrad.
He used his initials DSCH (D-Es-C-H in German) as a musical signature in several works.
